clinicalPearls: Caused by loss-of-function mutations in the BTK gene, arresting B-cell development at the pre-B stage so that mature B cells and immunoglobulin of all classes are profoundly deficient.
Affected boys typically present after 6 months of age once transplacental maternal IgG wanes, with recurrent sinopulmonary infections by encapsulated bacteria such as pneumococcus and Haemophilus.
Hallmark examination finding is absent or vestigial tonsils and lymph nodes because germinal centres cannot form without B cells.
Enteroviral infection is a feared complication, causing chronic meningoencephalitis and a dermatomyositis-like syndrome; live oral poliovirus vaccine is contraindicated.
Diagnosis rests on very low or absent circulating CD19+ B cells (usually under 2 percent) together with markedly reduced IgG, IgA and IgM.
Immunoglobulin replacement, given intravenously or subcutaneously, is the mainstay of therapy and dramatically reduces infection frequency.
Susceptibility to Giardia, Campylobacter, Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma is characteristic, and Pneumocystis is not typical because T-cell immunity is intact.
Bronchiectasis from recurrent or inadequately treated pulmonary infection remains the major cause of long-term morbidity.
reference.pathophysiology: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia results from mutations in the gene encoding Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK), a cytoplasmic signalling molecule essential for pre-B-cell receptor signalling. Without functional BTK, developing B lymphocytes cannot progress beyond the pro-B to pre-B transition in the bone marrow, so peripheral mature B cells are virtually absent. The consequent failure to generate plasma cells leaves the patient without effective antibody of any isotype, crippling humoral defence against encapsulated pyogenic bacteria and enteroviruses, while T-cell-mediated immunity is preserved. The X-linked recessive inheritance explains near-exclusive occurrence in males.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive agammaglobulinaemia (mu heavy chain, lambda-5, BLNK or Ig-alpha defects)
additionalInvestigations: Serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM) showing panhypogammaglobulinaemia
Peripheral blood lymphocyte immunophenotyping demonstrating absent CD19+/CD20+ B cells
BTK gene sequencing and assessment of BTK protein expression in monocytes
Specific antibody responses to protein and polysaccharide vaccines (absent)
High-resolution CT of the chest to detect bronchiectasis
Sputum and stool cultures for recurrent or atypical pathogens
Carrier testing and genetic counselling for female relatives
redFlags: Enteroviral central nervous system infection presenting with progressive encephalitis
Established bronchiectasis with declining pulmonary function
Chronic Giardia or Campylobacter infection with malabsorption and failure to thrive
Development of lymphoreticular or gastrointestinal malignancy
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis and lifelong immunoglobulin replacement most patients reach adulthood with a good quality of life, though chronic lung disease and enteroviral infection can shorten survival. Delayed recognition and consequent bronchiectasis are the principal determinants of poor outcome.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent infections in an infant to normal childhood illness and delaying immunological work-up.
Measuring immunoglobulins before 6 months when maternal IgG may mask the deficiency.
Administering live vaccines, particularly oral polio, which can cause vaccine-associated disease.
Under-dosing immunoglobulin replacement so that trough levels remain inadequate to prevent sinopulmonary infection.
Overlooking chronic enteroviral or ureaplasmal infection because routine cultures are negative.
references: Middleton's Allergy: Principles and Practice, current edition
International Union of Immunological Societies phenotypic classification of inborn errors of immunity
management: Immunoglobulin replacement given intravenously or subcutaneously is the mainstay, restoring humoral defence and markedly reducing infection frequency
Prompt, aggressive antibiotic treatment of bacterial infections, with prophylactic antibiotics considered for recurrent sinopulmonary disease
Avoidance of live vaccines, in particular oral poliovirus vaccine, because of the risk of vaccine-derived infection
Active surveillance for and management of bronchiectasis with airway clearance, interval CT and lung function monitoring
Vigilance for chronic enteroviral infection, including meningoencephalitis, given the specific vulnerability of this defect
Genetic counselling for this X-linked disorder with maternal carrier testing and family screening
Clinical immunology-led multidisciplinary follow-up to preserve lung function and detect complications early
